claim: Blood progenitors within the lymph gland are maintained by integrating signals emanating from niche-like cells and those from differentiating blood cells.
source: Blood progenitors within the lymph gland, a larval organ that supports hematopoiesis in Drosophila melanogaster, are maintained by integrating signals emanating from niche-like cells and those from differentiating blood cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a summary of the biological system being studied.

claim: The signal from differentiating cells is termed the 'equilibrium signal' to distinguish it from the 'niche signal'.
source: We term the signal from differentiating cells the 'equilibrium signal' in order to distinguish it from the 'niche signal'.
evidence: This is a definitional statement made by the authors in the abstract.

claim: Equilibrium signaling utilizes Pvr (the Drosophila PDGF/VEGF receptor), STAT92E, and adenosine deaminase-related growth factor A (ADGF-A).
source: Earlier we showed that equilibrium signaling utilizes Pvr (the Drosophila PDGF/VEGF receptor), STAT92E, and adenosine deaminase-related growth factor A (ADGF-A) (Mondal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: bip1 (bric à brac interacting protein 1) is a regulator of the equilibrium signal.
source: To identify new genes involved in lymph gland blood progenitor maintenance, particularly those involved in equilibrium signaling, we performed a genetic screen that identified bip1 (bric à brac interacting protein 1) and Nucleoporin 98 (Nup98) as additional regulators of the equilibrium signal.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic screen described in the manuscript.

claim: Nucleoporin 98 (Nup98) is a regulator of the equilibrium signal.
source: To identify new genes involved in lymph gland blood progenitor maintenance, particularly those involved in equilibrium signaling, we performed a genetic screen that identified bip1 (bric à brac interacting protein 1) and Nucleoporin 98 (Nup98) as additional regulators of the equilibrium signal.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the genetic screen described in the manuscript.

claim: The products of bip1, Nup98, and RpS8 (Ribosomal protein S8) are required for the proper expression of Pvr.
source: We show that the products of these genes along with the Bip1-interacting protein RpS8 (Ribosomal protein S8) are required for the proper expression of Pvr.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: Blood cell differentiation in Drosophila is regulated in the head mesoderm of the embryo.
source: Similar to vertebrates, blood cell differentiation in Drosophila is regulated in multiple hematopoietic environments, which include the head mesoderm of the embryo (Tepass et al., 1994; Lebestky et al., 2000; Milchanowski et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Blood cell differentiation in Drosophila is regulated in the specialized, tissue-associated microenvironments of the larval periphery (e.g, body wall hematopoietic pockets).
source: Similar to vertebrates, blood cell differentiation in Drosophila is regulated in multiple hematopoietic environments, which include the head mesoderm of the embryo (Tepass et al., 1994; Lebestky et al., 2000; Milchanowski et al., 2004), the specialized, tissue-associated microenvironments of the larval periphery (e.g, body wall hematopoietic pockets) (Markus et al., 2009; Makhijani et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Blood cell differentiation in Drosophila is regulated in the larval lymph gland.
source: Similar to vertebrates, blood cell differentiation in Drosophila is regulated in multiple hematopoietic environments, which include the head mesoderm of the embryo (Tepass et al., 1994; Lebestky et al., 2000; Milchanowski et al., 2004), the specialized, tissue-associated microenvironments of the larval periphery (e.g, body wall hematopoietic pockets) (Markus et al., 2009; Makhijani et al., 2011), and the larval lymph gland, an organ dedicated to the development of blood cells that normally contribute to the pupal and adult stages (Rizki, 1978; Shrestha and Gateff, 1982; Lanot et al., 2001; Jung et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Differentiating blood cells (hemocytes) of the lymph gland are derived from multipotent progenitors.
source: Differentiating blood cells (hemocytes) of the lymph gland are derived from multipotent progenitors (Jung et al., 2005; Mandal et al., 2007; Martinez-Agosto et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Blood progenitors readily proliferate during the early growth phases of lymph gland development.
source: These blood progenitors readily proliferate during the early growth phases of lymph gland development, which is followed by a period in which many of these cells slow their rate of division and are maintained without differentiation in a region termed the medullary zone (MZ, Figure 1) (Jung et al., 2005; Mandal et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Blood progenitors are maintained without differentiation in a region termed the medullary zone (MZ).
source: These blood progenitors readily proliferate during the early growth phases of lymph gland development, which is followed by a period in which many of these cells slow their rate of division and are maintained without differentiation in a region termed the medullary zone (MZ, Figure 1) (Jung et al., 2005; Mandal et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1.

claim: Progenitor cells begin to differentiate along the peripheral edge of the lymph gland to give rise to a separate cortical zone (CZ).
source: During the same period, other progenitor cells begin to differentiate along the peripheral edge of the lymph gland to give rise to a separate cortical zone (CZ) (Jung et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Wingless (Wg; Wnt in vertebrates) is expressed by blood progenitor cells in the lymph gland.
source: Wingless (Wg; Wnt in vertebrates) is expressed by blood progenitor cells in the lymph gland and has an important role in promoting their maintenance (Sinenko et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Wingless has an important role in promoting blood progenitor cell maintenance.
source: Wingless (Wg; Wnt in vertebrates) is expressed by blood progenitor cells in the lymph gland and has an important role in promoting their maintenance (Sinenko et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) function in progenitor cells to potentiate blood progenitor differentiation both in the context of normal development and during oxidative stress.
source: and reactive oxygen species (ROS) function in these cells to potentiate blood progenitor differentiation both in the context of normal development and during oxidative stress (Owusu-Ansah and Banerjee, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Progenitor cell maintenance at late developmental stages is dependent upon Hedgehog (Hh) signaling from the posterior signaling center (PSC).
source: Progenitor cell maintenance at late developmental stages is also dependent upon Hedgehog (Hh) signaling from a small population of cells called the posterior signaling center that functions as a hematopoietic niche (PSC) (Lebestky et al., 2003; Jung et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The posterior signaling center (PSC) functions as a hematopoietic niche.
source: Progenitor cell maintenance at late developmental stages is also dependent upon Hedgehog (Hh) signaling from a small population of cells called the posterior signaling center that functions as a hematopoietic niche (PSC) (Lebestky et al., 2003; Jung et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The maintenance of lymph gland blood progenitors requires a backward signal arising from the differentiating cells.
source: More recently, it has been discovered that the maintenance of lymph gland blood progenitors also requires a backward signal arising from the differentiating cells (Mondal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The backward signal from differentiating cells is controlled by a pathway that combines the function of the receptor tyrosine kinase Pvr and JAK-independent STAT (STAT92E) activation in differentiating cells, followed by the expression of ADGF-A.
source: This signal is controlled by a novel pathway that combines the function of the receptor tyrosine kinase Pvr and JAK-independent STAT (STAT92E) activation in differentiating cells, followed by the expression of ADGF-A (Figure 1), a secreted enzyme that converts adenosine to inosine (Mondal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and reference to Figure 1.

claim: ADGF-A is a secreted enzyme that converts adenosine to inosine.
source: This signal is controlled by a novel pathway that combines the function of the receptor tyrosine kinase Pvr and JAK-independent STAT (STAT92E) activation in differentiating cells, followed by the expression of ADGF-A (Figure 1), a secreted enzyme that converts adenosine to inosine (Mondal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Extracellular adenosine is a well-established signal in mammalian systems in various contexts, particularly stress conditions.
source: Extracellular adenosine is a well-established signal in mammalian systems in various contexts, particularly stress conditions (Fredholm, 2007; Sheth et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: An elevated adenosine level in Drosophila causes extensive blood cell proliferation.
source: and an elevated adenosine level in Drosophila causes extensive blood cell proliferation (Dolezal et al., 2005; Mondal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Differentiating and mature cells express (and are the primary source of) ADGF-A.
source: It has been demonstrated that differentiating and mature cells express (and are the primary source of) ADGF-A, and that its enzymatic activity (which converts adenosine to inosine) is required for progenitor cell maintenance (Mondal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ADGF-A enzymatic activity (which converts adenosine to inosine) is required for progenitor cell maintenance.
source: It has been demonstrated that differentiating and mature cells express (and are the primary source of) ADGF-A, and that its enzymatic activity (which converts adenosine to inosine) is required for progenitor cell maintenance (Mondal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: As differentiation proceeds, ADGF-A expression (activity) increasingly promotes the maintenance of extant blood progenitors through the reduction of stimulatory adenosine.
source: As differentiation proceeds, ADGF-A expression (activity) increasingly promotes the maintenance of extant blood progenitors through the reduction of stimulatory adenosine.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the equilibrium signaling model.

claim: Loss of ADGF-A from differentiating cells increases extracellular adenosine level.
source: Loss of ADGF-A (or STAT or Pvr) from differentiating cells increases extracellular adenosine level and thereby increases Adenosine Receptor (AdoR) signaling and downstream Protein Kinase A (PKA) activity in progenitors, which causes these cells to proliferate (Dolezal et al., 2005; Mondal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Loss of STAT from differentiating cells increases extracellular adenosine level.
source: Loss of ADGF-A (or STAT or Pvr) from differentiating cells increases extracellular adenosine level and thereby increases Adenosine Receptor (AdoR) signaling and downstream Protein Kinase A (PKA) activity in progenitors, which causes these cells to proliferate (Dolezal et al., 2005; Mondal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Loss of Pvr from differentiating cells increases extracellular adenosine level.
source: Loss of ADGF-A (or STAT or Pvr) from differentiating cells increases extracellular adenosine level and thereby increases Adenosine Receptor (AdoR) signaling and downstream Protein Kinase A (PKA) activity in progenitors, which causes these cells to proliferate (Dolezal et al., 2005; Mondal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Increased extracellular adenosine increases Adenosine Receptor (AdoR) signaling and downstream Protein Kinase A (PKA) activity in progenitors, which causes these cells to proliferate.
source: Loss of ADGF-A (or STAT or Pvr) from differentiating cells increases extracellular adenosine level and thereby increases Adenosine Receptor (AdoR) signaling and downstream Protein Kinase A (PKA) activity in progenitors, which causes these cells to proliferate (Dolezal et al., 2005; Mondal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PKA is a central regulator of progenitor maintenance because it integrates input from both the equilibrium signal (ADGF-A) and the niche signal (Hh).
source: PKA is a central regulator of progenitor maintenance because it integrates input from both the equilibrium signal (ADGF-A) and the niche signal (Hh).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the signaling model.

claim: PKA mediates the conversion of the transcriptional regulator Cubitus interruptus (Ci, a homolog of vertebrate Gli) from its full length form (Ci155), required for progenitor maintenance, to a cleaved form (Ci75) that promotes proliferation.
source: PKA mediates the conversion of the transcriptional regulator Cubitus interruptus (Ci, a homolog of vertebrate Gli) from its full length form (Ci155), required for progenitor maintenance (Mandal et al., 2007), to a cleaved form (Ci75) that promotes proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Signaling by Hh inhibits PKA and promotes Ci155 stabilization.
source: Signaling by Hh inhibits PKA and promotes Ci155 stabilization whereas adenosine/AdoR signaling activates PKA and promotes Ci75 conversion.
evidence: This is a mechanistic description of the signaling pathway.

claim: Adenosine/AdoR signaling activates PKA and promotes Ci75 conversion.
source: Signaling by Hh inhibits PKA and promotes Ci155 stabilization whereas adenosine/AdoR signaling activates PKA and promotes Ci75 conversion.
evidence: This is a mechanistic description of the signaling pathway.

claim: Both Hh (the niche signal) and ADGF-A (the equilibrium signal which removes adenosine) limit PKA activity and promote progenitor cell maintenance.
source: Thus, both Hh (the niche signal) and ADGF-A (the equilibrium signal which removes adenosine) limit PKA activity and promote progenitor cell maintenance.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the signaling mechanism.

claim: The HHLT-gal4 line labels the hematopoietic system by Gal4-dependent expression of EGFP, such that it can be visualized in live, whole animals.
source: To circumvent this barrier to genetic screening, we generated a line of flies termed the Hand-Hemolectin Lineage Traced-gal4 line (HHLT-gal4 UAS-2XEGFP, Figure 2A; see 'Materials and methods' for precise genotype) in which the hematopoietic system is labeled by Gal4-dependent expression of EGFP, such that it can be visualized in live, whole animals (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is a description of the tool developed for the screen, supported by Figure 2.

claim: The HHLT-gal4 line makes use of two gal4 drivers to target early lymph gland blood cells (hemocytes; Hand-gal4) and circulating and sessile blood cells (Hemolectin-gal4 or Hml-gal4).
source: This line makes use of two gal4 drivers to target early lymph gland blood cells (hemocytes; Hand-gal4) and circulating and sessile blood cells (Hemolectin-gal4 or Hml-gal4) and incorporates a Gal4/FLP recombinase-dependent cell lineage tracing cassette to maintain Gal4 expression in the lymph gland after the Hand-gal4 driver itself is down-regulated during the first instar.
evidence: This is a description of the genetic components of the HHLT-gal4 line.

claim: The HHLT-gal4 line incorporates a Gal4/FLP recombinase-dependent cell lineage tracing cassette to maintain Gal4 expression in the lymph gland after the Hand-gal4 driver itself is down-regulated during the first instar.
source: This line makes use of two gal4 drivers to target early lymph gland blood cells (hemocytes; Hand-gal4) and circulating and sessile blood cells (Hemolectin-gal4 or Hml-gal4) and incorporates a Gal4/FLP recombinase-dependent cell lineage tracing cassette to maintain Gal4 expression in the lymph gland after the Hand-gal4 driver itself is down-regulated during the first instar.
evidence: This is a description of the genetic components of the HHLT-gal4 line.

claim: The Hand-gal4 driver is expressed in the embryonic cardiogenic mesoderm from which the lymph gland is derived.
source: The Hand-gal4 driver is expressed in the embryonic cardiogenic mesoderm from which the lymph gland is derived.
evidence: This is a description of the expression pattern of Hand-gal4.

claim: The dorsal vessel (heart) cardioblasts and the pericardial nephrocytes are marked by the cell lineage tracing cassette in HHLT-gal4.
source: Therefore, the dorsal vessel (heart) cardioblasts and the pericardial nephrocytes are also marked by the cell lineage tracing cassette (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a description of the expression pattern of HHLT-gal4, supported by Figure 2B.

claim: EGFP is not expressed in other larval tissues in HHLT-gal4, except in the late third-instar salivary glands.
source: EGFP is not expressed in other larval tissues, except in the late third-instar salivary glands that are readily discernible from the hematopoietic system (Figure 2B,E).
evidence: This is a description of the expression pattern of HHLT-gal4, supported by Figure 2.

claim: A screen was conducted in which HHLT-gal4 was used to independently misexpress 503 unique UAS-controlled Drosophila genes.
source: A screen was conducted in which HHLT-gal4 was used to independently misexpress 503 unique UAS-controlled Drosophila genes, with their effects on the hematopoietic system assessed in whole animals based upon EGFP expression.
evidence: This is a description of the screening methodology.

claim: When crossed to HHLT-gal4, 281 of the LA lines cause a scorable phenotype in either lymph glands or circulating blood cells of late third-instar larvae.
source: When crossed to HHLT-gal4, 281 of these lines cause a scorable phenotype in either lymph glands or circulating blood cells of late third-instar larvae (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from the misexpression screen.

claim: LA line 527, which is predicted to misexpress Ras85D, causes a robust expansion of the lymph gland.
source: As an example, LA line 527, which is predicted to misexpress Ras85D, causes a robust expansion of the lymph gland (Figure 2D), consistent with the previously identified role of Ras85D in controlling hemocyte proliferation (Asha et al., 2003; Sinenko and Mathey-Prevot, 2004).
evidence: This is a result from the misexpression screen, supported by Figure 2D and citations.

claim: LA line 630 misexpresses the gene combgap (encoding a zinc finger transcription factor) and causes a strong reduction in lymph gland size.
source: By contrast, LA line 630 misexpresses the gene combgap (encoding a zinc finger transcription factor) and causes a strong reduction in lymph gland size (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a result from the misexpression screen, supported by Figure 2E.

claim: 73 RNAi lines targeting 69 genes alter lymph gland size or morphology when crossed to HHLT-gal4.
source: We were able to obtain RNAi lines targeting 251 of the candidate genes identified by misexpression and found that 73 RNAi lines targeting 69 genes alter lymph gland size or morphology when crossed to HHLT-gal4 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from the RNAi screen.

claim: In wild-type lymph glands, expression of mature cell markers such as Pxn is restricted to the periphery of the primary lobe (the cortical zone).
source: In wild-type lymph glands, expression of mature cell markers such as Pxn is restricted to the periphery of the primary lobe (the cortical zone) (Jung et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a description of normal lymph gland organization, supported by citation.

claim: When niche signaling or equilibrium signaling are compromised, progenitor cells are lost and differentiation markers, including Pxn, are expressed throughout the lymph gland primary lobes.
source: By contrast, when niche signaling or equilibrium signaling are compromised, progenitor cells are lost and differentiation markers, including Pxn, are expressed throughout the lymph gland primary lobes (Mandal et al., 2007; Mondal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a description of the phenotype when signaling is disrupted, supported by citations.

claim: Rescreening the 73 identified RNAi lines using HHLT-gal4 identified 20 genes (21 RNAi lines) that, when knocked down, cause the expression of Pxn in cells throughout the lymph gland primary lobe.
source: Rescreening the 73 identified RNAi lines using HHLT-gal4 identified 20 genes (21 RNAi lines) that, when knocked down, cause the expression of Pxn in cells throughout the lymph gland primary lobe (Figure 3; Table 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from the RNAi screen, supported by Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The progenitor population (Pxn negative) is either strongly reduced or absent in each RNAi background that causes expanded Pxn expression.
source: Compared to controls, the progenitor population (Pxn negative) is either strongly reduced or absent in each RNAi background.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the RNAi screen results.

claim: Targeting RNAi to differentiating and mature cells using Hml-gal4 identified six genes (CG6854 [CTPsyn], CG7398 [Transportin], CG7574 [bip1], CG10009 [Noa36], CG10198 [Nup98, also known as Nup98-96], and CG31938 [Rrp40]) that cause an expansion of Pxn.
source: Targeting RNAi to differentiating and mature cells using Hml-gal4 (Sinenko and Mathey-Prevot, 2004) identified six genes (CG6854 [CTPsyn], CG7398 [Transportin], CG7574 [bip1], CG10009 [Noa36], CG10198 [Nup98, also known as Nup98-96], and CG31938 [Rrp40]) that cause an expansion of Pxn (Figure 4A–G) and Hml-gal4, UAS EGFP (Figure 4H–M) expression.
evidence: This is a result from the zone-specific RNAi screen, supported by Figure 4.

claim: The six genes identified by Hml-gal4 screening encode likely candidates for new components of the equilibrium signaling pathway.
source: Since the function of these genes is needed in the CZ for the maintenance of the MZ progenitors, these six genes encode likely candidates for new components of the equilibrium signaling pathway.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the zone-specific screening results.

claim: Screening with dome-gal4 to target RNAi to the progenitor cells identified eleven genes.
source: Screening with dome-gal4 (Jung et al., 2005) to target RNAi to the progenitor cells identified eleven genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–L), three of which (Transportin, Noa36, and Rrp40) are in common with those identified using Hml-gal4.
evidence: This is a result from the zone-specific RNAi screen, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Use of Antennapedia-gal4 (Antp-gal4) to target RNAi specifically to niche cells failed to identify any of the 21 lines as additional niche signaling components.
source: By contrast, use of Antennapedia-gal4 (Antp-gal4) (Mandal et al., 2007) to target RNAi specifically to niche cells failed to identify any of the 21 lines as additional niche signaling components (not shown).
evidence: This is a result from the zone-specific RNAi screen.

claim: Seven of the 21 RNAi lines did not cause a phenotype when expressed with any of the zone-specific Gal4 driver lines used.
source: Lastly, seven of the 21 RNAi lines did not cause a phenotype when expressed with any of the zone-specific Gal4 driver lines used.
evidence: This is a result from the zone-specific RNAi screen.

claim: CTPsyn, bip1, and Nup98 cause a loss of lymph gland progenitor cells upon RNAi knock down in differentiating cells, but not in progenitor cells or in niche cells.
source: Taken together, our screen identified three genes, CTPsyn, bip1, and Nup98, which cause a loss of lymph gland progenitor cells upon RNAi knock down in differentiating cells, but not in progenitor cells or in niche cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the zone-specific screening results.

claim: The bip1 gene was originally identified through a yeast two-hybrid screen that showed that its encoded protein binds the BTB/POZ domain of the transcription factor Bric à brac 1 (Bab1).
source: The bip1 gene was originally identified through a yeast two-hybrid screen that showed that its encoded protein binds the BTB/POZ domain of the transcription factor Bric à brac 1 (Bab1) (Pointud et al., 2001), a protein that has several developmental roles including the formation of ovarian terminal filament cells that are required for germline stem cell maintenance (Lin and Spradling, 1993; Sahut-Barnola et al., 1995; Couderc et al., 2002).
evidence: This is background information about bip1, supported by citations.

claim: Bab1 has several developmental roles including the formation of ovarian terminal filament cells that are required for germline stem cell maintenance.
source: The bip1 gene was originally identified through a yeast two-hybrid screen that showed that its encoded protein binds the BTB/POZ domain of the transcription factor Bric à brac 1 (Bab1) (Pointud et al., 2001), a protein that has several developmental roles including the formation of ovarian terminal filament cells that are required for germline stem cell maintenance (Lin and Spradling, 1993; Sahut-Barnola et al., 1995; Couderc et al., 2002).
evidence: This is background information about Bab1, supported by citations.

claim: Analysis of the predicted Bip1 amino acid sequence identifies a THAP domain containing a C2CH-type zinc finger motif that is known to bind DNA.
source: Analysis of the predicted Bip1 amino acid sequence (InterPro) (Hunter et al., 2012) identifies a THAP domain containing a C2CH-type zinc finger motif that is known to bind DNA (Sabogal et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a description of Bip1 protein structure, supported by citations.

claim: RNAi knock down of bip1 using Hml-gal4 reduces bip1 mRNA levels in the lymph gland to approximately ten percent of that observed in controls.
source: Indeed, RNAi knock down of bip1 using Hml-gal4 (Sinenko and Mathey-Prevot, 2004; Jung et al., 2005) reduces bip1 mRNA levels in the lymph gland to approximately ten percent of that observed in controls (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a result from qRT-PCR validation, supported by Figure 5A.

claim: The bip1 RNAi blood phenotype is suppressible by the simultaneous overexpression of bip1.
source: The bip1 RNAi blood phenotype is also suppressible by the simultaneous overexpression of bip1 (UAS-bip1LA645; Figure 5B–B'), demonstrating the specific requirement for bip1 in maintaining progenitors.
evidence: This is a result from genetic rescue experiments, supported by Figure 5B-B'.

claim: Driving bip1 RNAi with Pxn-gal4 causes the loss of progenitor cells.
source: Driving bip1 RNAi with Pxn-gal4, an alternative differentiating- and mature-cell driver to Hml-gal4, also causes the loss of progenitor cells (Figure 5C–C′), thereby confirming that bip1 knock-down in differentiating cells is key to its associated phenotype.
evidence: This is a result from zone-specific RNAi experiments, supported by Figure 5C-C'.

claim: The progenitor cell marker dome-MESO-lacZ is strongly reduced relative to control lymph glands in the bip1 RNAi (Hml-gal4) background.
source: Additionally, the progenitor cell marker dome-MESO-lacZ (Hombria et al., 2005; Krzemien et al., 2007) is strongly reduced relative to control lymph glands (Figure 5D–D′) in the bip1 RNAi (Hml-gal4) background.
evidence: This is a result from marker analysis, supported by Figure 5D-D'.

claim: RpS8 has been identified in genomic-scale yeast two-hybrid analyses as a Bip1-interacting protein.
source: Interestingly, RpS8 has also been identified in genomic-scale yeast two-hybrid analyses as a Bip1-interacting protein (Giot et al., 2003; Formstecher et al., 2005; Stark et al., 2006)
evidence: This is background information about RpS8, supported by citations.

claim: RNAi knockdown of RpS8 causes the expanded expression of both Pxn and Hml-gal4 UAS-GFP expression throughout the lymph gland primary lobes.
source: Consistent with this idea, RNAi knockdown of RpS8 also causes the expanded expression of both Pxn and Hml-gal4 UAS-GFP expression throughout the lymph gland primary lobes (Figure 5E–E′).
evidence: This is a result from RNAi experiments, supported by Figure 5E-E'.

claim: Knockdown of RpS8 directly in niche or progenitor cells (using Antp-gal4 and dome-gal4, respectively) does not cause their loss to differentiation.
source: This result reflects a specific function of RpS8 in these cells because knockdown directly in niche or progenitor cells (using Antp-gal4 and dome-gal4, respectively) does not cause their loss to differentiation (not shown).
evidence: This is a result from zone-specific RNAi experiments.

claim: Overexpression of either activated STAT (STATACT) or ADGF-A in differentiating cells can suppress the Pvr loss-of-function phenotype.
source: The progenitor maintenance function of Pvr signaling in differentiated cells requires the downstream function of the STAT transcriptional activator and the secreted enzyme ADGF-A (Mondal et al., 2011), and, consistent with this relationship, overexpression of either activated STAT (STATACT) (Ekas et al., 2010) or ADGF-A in differentiating cells can suppress the Pvr loss-of-function phenotype (Mondal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is background information about the equilibrium signaling pathway, supported by citations.

claim: Overexpression of STATACT or ADGF-A can suppress the bip1 RNAi phenotype.
source: Likewise, we find that overexpression of STATACT or ADGF-A can suppress the bip1 RNAi phenotype (Figure 6A–D′).
evidence: This is a result from genetic suppression experiments, supported by Figure 6A-D'.

claim: Overexpression of Pvr strongly suppresses the bip1 RNAi phenotype, returning lymph gland morphology and organization to essentially wild type.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of Pvr also strongly suppresses the bip1 RNAi phenotype, returning lymph gland morphology and organization to essentially wild type (Figure 6E–E′).
evidence: This is a result from genetic suppression experiments, supported by Figure 6E-E'.

claim: Overexpression of bip1 does not suppress the Pvr RNAi phenotype.
source: By contrast, overexpression of bip1 does not suppress the Pvr RNAi phenotype (Hml-gal4 UAS-Pvr RNAi UAS-bip1LA645; not shown).
evidence: This is a result from genetic suppression experiments.

claim: bip1 function is genetically upstream of Pvr and other equilibrium signaling components in lymph gland progenitor maintenance by differentiating cells.
source: Collectively, these results place bip1 function genetically upstream of Pvr and other equilibrium signaling components in lymph gland progenitor maintenance by differentiating cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the genetic suppression results.

claim: A reduction in Pvr protein expression within the lymph gland is observed in the bip1 RNAi background by mid-second instar, soon after differentiation begins (∼40 hr post-hatching).
source: Indeed, a reduction in Pvr protein expression within the lymph gland is observed in the bip1 RNAi background by mid-second instar, soon after differentiation begins (∼40 hr post-hatching; Figure 6F–J′).
evidence: This is a result from immunostaining experiments, supported by Figure 6F-J'.

claim: By the late third instar, Pvr protein levels in the lymph gland remain strongly reduced in bip1 RNAi backgrounds.
source: By the late third instar (when the bip1 RNAi differentiation phenotype is most apparent), Pvr protein levels in the lymph gland remain strongly reduced (Figure 6J–J′).
evidence: This is a result from immunostaining experiments, supported by Figure 6J-J'.

claim: Knockdown of bip1 function in lymph glands by Hml-gal4-mediated RNAi reduces lymph gland Pvr transcript levels to approximately 70% of control levels.
source: Knockdown of bip1 function in lymph glands by Hml-gal4-mediated RNAi reduces lymph gland Pvr transcript levels to approximately 70% of control levels (assessed by qRT-PCR; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is a result from qRT-PCR experiments, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: bip1 RNAi in circulating blood cells reduces Pvr transcript level to approximately 35% of the control level.
source: In support of this idea, bip1 RNAi in circulating blood cells (where greater than 90% express Hml-gal4) reduces Pvr transcript level to approximately 35% of the control level (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a result from qRT-PCR experiments, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Expression of bip1 RNAi in FLP-out Gal4-expressing cell clones made exclusively in the lymph gland strongly reduces Pvr levels compared to nearby cells not expressing RNAi as well as to mock clones.
source: Expression of bip1 RNAi in FLP-out Gal4-expressing cell clones made exclusively in the lymph gland strongly reduces Pvr levels compared to nearby cells not expressing RNAi as well as to mock clones (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C)
evidence: This is a result from clonal analysis experiments, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: bip1 RNAi expression with srpHemo-gal4 does not reduce lymph gland Pvr levels.
source: Furthermore, bip1 RNAi expression with srpHemo-gal4 (Bruckner et al., 2004), which expresses in a large fraction of circulating cells but in few or no cells within the lymph gland, does not reduce lymph gland Pvr levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E–H).
evidence: This is a result from zone-specific RNAi experiments, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2E-H.

claim: bip1 is required for proper Pvr protein expression, and therefore proper equilibrium signaling, within the developing lymph gland.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that bip1 is required for proper Pvr protein expression, and therefore proper equilibrium signaling, within the developing lymph gland.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the bip1 experiments.

claim: RpS8 RNAi reduces Pvr protein expression in the lymph gland.
source: This effect is likely due to the loss of equilibrium signaling during development since RpS8 RNAi also reduces Pvr protein expression in the lymph gland (Figure 6K–K′).
evidence: This is a result from immunostaining experiments, supported by Figure 6K-K'.

claim: Knockdown of RpS8 by RNAi reduces Pvr transcript levels.
source: Knockdown of RpS8 by RNAi, as with knockdown of bip1, also reduces Pvr transcript levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a result from qRT-PCR experiments, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: A Drosophila RNAi screen using the blood-related S2 cell line previously identified both Pvr and RpS8 as regulators of cell size and division.
source: Interestingly, a Drosophila RNAi screen using the blood-related S2 cell line previously identified both Pvr and RpS8 as regulators of cell size and division (Sims et al., 2009).
evidence: This is background information from a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: Nup98 knockdown in differentiating cells specifically causes a loss of progenitors cells.
source: In addition to bip1, the screen described here identified Nup98 as a potential equilibrium signaling component because its knockdown in differentiating cells specifically causes a loss of progenitors cells (Figure 3T and Figure 4F–F′′).
evidence: This is a result from the RNAi screen, supported by Figures 3T and 4F-F''.

claim: Nup98 and other nuclear pore components such as Sec13 and Nup88 can regulate gene expression through the binding of target promoters.
source: Although Nup98 is widely known as a general component of the nuclear pore complex, recent work has demonstrated that Nup98 and other nuclear pore components such as Sec13 and Nup88, can regulate gene expression through the binding of target promoters (Capelson et al., 2010; Kalverda et al., 2010; Liang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is background information about Nup98, supported by citations.

claim: Chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments identified bip1, RpS8, and the equilibrium signaling genes Pvr and STAT (STAT92E) as in vivo Nup98 regulatory targets.
source: Moreover, chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments identified bip1, RpS8, and the equilibrium signaling genes Pvr and STAT (STAT92E) as in vivo Nup98 regulatory targets (Capelson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is background information from a previous study, supported by citation.

claim: Nup98 knockdown specifically in differentiating cells of lymph glands causes a strong reduction in Pvr expression.
source: Consistent with a function in regulation of equilibrium signaling genes, Nup98 knockdown specifically in differentiating cells of lymph glands causes a strong reduction in Pvr expression (Figure 6L–L′).
evidence: This is a result from immunostaining experiments, supported by Figure 6L-L'.

claim: RNAi knockdown of the nucleoporin Sec13 in differentiating cells has no effect on the maintenance of progenitor cells or Pvr expression.
source: By contrast, RNAi knockdown of the nucleoporin Sec13 in differentiating cells has no effect on the maintenance of progenitor cells or Pvr expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is a result from RNAi experiments, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Single-copy loss of Nup98 and Pvr in combination causes extensive loss of progenitor cells to differentiation.
source: Furthermore, the close genetic relationship between Nup98 and Pvr is illustrated by the fact that single-copy loss of these genes in combination causes extensive loss of progenitor cells to differentiation (Figure 6M–M′).
evidence: This is a result from genetic interaction experiments, supported by Figure 6M-M'.

claim: Overexpression of bip1 in Nup98 RNAi lymph glands is sufficient to restore Pvr protein expression and to suppress the loss of progenitors to differentiation.
source: Interestingly, overexpression of bip1 in Nup98 RNAi lymph glands (Hml-gal4 UAS-Nup98 RNAi UAS-bip1LA645) is sufficient to restore Pvr protein expression and to suppress the loss of progenitors to differentiation (based upon lymph gland morphology and Hml-gal4 expression; Figure 6N–N′).
evidence: This is a result from genetic rescue experiments, supported by Figure 6N-N'.

claim: Pvr expression is normal in collier (col) mutant lymph glands, which lack niche signaling and are strongly differentiated by late larval stages.
source: To test this, Pvr expression was examined in collier (col) mutant lymph glands, which lack niche signaling and are strongly differentiated by late larval stages (Crozatier et al., 2004; Mandal et al., 2007), and was found to be normal (Figure 6—figure supplement 4, compare with Pvr expression in wild-type cortical zone differentiating cells in Figure 6F′).
evidence: This is a result from mutant analysis, supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Pvr requires bip1, RpS8, and Nup98 for proper developmental expression in the lymph gland.
source: Thus, Pvr requires bip1, RpS8, and Nup98 for proper developmental expression in the lymph gland.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Bip1, RpS8, and Nup98 are independently required for the expression of Pvr.
source: Bip1, RpS8, and Nup98 are independently required for the expression of Pvr (direct arrows).
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 7.

claim: Rescue of endogenous Pvr expression by misexpression of bip1 in the Nup98 RNAi background indicates that bip1 functions genetically downstream of Nup98 in the control of Pvr expression.
source: Rescue of endogenous Pvr expression by misexpression of bip1 in the Nup98 RNAi background indicates that bip1 functions genetically downstream of Nup98 (dashed arrow) in the control of Pvr expression.
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 7 and is based on the rescue experiment.

claim: Bip1 and RpS8 may work together in a complex to control Pvr expression in vivo.
source: Bip1 and RpS8 may work together in a complex (dashed line) to control Pvr expression in vivo.
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 7 and is based on the yeast two-hybrid data.

claim: The predicted Bip1 protein exhibits only one recognizable structural sequence, namely a THAP domain that contains a putative DNA-binding zinc finger motif.
source: The predicted Bip1 protein exhibits only one recognizable structural sequence, namely a THAP domain that contains a putative DNA-binding zinc finger motif.
evidence: This is a description of Bip1 protein structure.

claim: Bip1 behaves as a positive regulator of Pvr transcription.
source: Our results suggest that Bip1 behaves as a positive regulator of Pvr transcription, but whether this occurs directly through Bip1 interaction with the Pvr locus will require further investigation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The identification of Bip1 and Nup98 as regulators of hematopoietic progenitors in Drosophila may be indicative of important conserved functions of related proteins within the vertebrate blood lineages.
source: The identification of Bip1 and Nup98 as regulators of hematopoietic progenitors in Drosophila may be indicative of important conserved functions of related proteins within the vertebrate blood lineages similar to what has been shown previously for GATA, FOG, and RUNX factors (Waltzer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential conservation of function.

claim: THAP-domain proteins are conserved across species and have been reported to have a variety of important functions in mammalian systems, including maintenance of murine embryonic stem cell pluripotency.
source: THAP-domain proteins are conserved across species and have been reported to have a variety of important functions in mammalian systems, including maintenance of murine embryonic stem cell pluripotency (Cayrol et al., 2007; Dejosez et al., 2008, 2010).
evidence: This is background information about THAP-domain proteins, supported by citations.

claim: Mutations in the human THAP1 gene have been associated with dystonia.
source: With regard to the diseased state, mutations in the human THAP1 gene have been associated with dystonia (Fuchs et al., 2009; Paisan-Ruiz et al., 2009; Kaiser et al., 2010; Mazars et al., 2010), a neuromuscular disorder that causes repetitive, involuntary muscular contraction
evidence: This is background information about THAP1, supported by citations.

claim: THAP1/Par4 protein complexes have been shown to promote apoptosis in leukemic blood cells in various experimental contexts in vitro.
source: and THAP1/Par4 protein complexes have been shown to promote apoptosis in leukemic blood cells in various experimental contexts in vitro (Lu et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is background information about THAP1, supported by citations.

claim: Chromosomal translocations that generate Nup98 fusion proteins have been implicated in numerous human myelodysplastic syndromes and leukemias.
source: Chromosomal translocations that generate Nup98 fusion proteins have been implicated in numerous human myelodysplastic syndromes and leukemias (Nishiyama et al., 1999; Ahuja et al., 2001; Lin et al., 2005; Nakamura, 2005; van Zutven et al., 2006; Slape et al., 2008; Kaltenbach et al., 2010; Murayama et al., 2013)
evidence: This is background information about Nup98, supported by citations.
